newsitem.title: USA: IRS official says agency victim in yield burning.
newsitem.headline: IRS official says agency victim in yield burning.

text.p: The Internal Revenue Service got a "bum" deal as a result of yield burning in the municipal bond market and it has no place to go but to bond issuers and investors to get its money back, an IRS official said Friday.

"The way we look at is that we got a bum check and we turned that check over to see who endorsed it and we find that the issuer did," Gerald Sack, chief of technical branch four in IRS' exempt organizations division, said in response to charges leveled by a National League of Cities official May 8.

In a speech before bond lawyers meeting here, League federal relations chief Frank Shafroth likened the IRS' strategy for collecting lost yield burning dollars to fining the passenger in a taxicab for a traffic violation committed by the cab driver.

Yield burning refers to allegations that bond underwriters overcharge states and localities for U.S. Treasury securities they bought to help them refinance outstanding bonds. The IRS says localities can enter into closing agreements with the Service on such deals to head off any enforcement action by the Service.

IRS' Sack told the bond lawyers on Friday: "The federal government is missing millions if not billions of dollars" because of yield burning. "It's our mandate to recover the money that is responsibly owed to the federal government."
Sack said the IRS has no other option under federal law, but to seek the money from the entity that issued the bonds, not the firms that underwrote them.

"The statute directs us to the bondholder," Sack said. "So if we find there's yield burning and then we find there's (a) markup problem, then we are instructed by statute to go to the bondholders. That is IRS' "first shot."
